headline: A small office for
buildings that *take*
their time.
paragraphs: Studio Morfis was founded in 2011 by Astrid Morfis. We are fourteen people working on a deliberately small number of projects at a time.
Our work spans private houses, cultural and sacred buildings, and public housing. The scale changes; the questions stay the same: mass, light, and how a room will feel in forty years.

principles.title: Subtract before adding
principles.body: We begin by asking what a building can do without. Most of our best rooms are made by removing.

principles.title: Let structure finish
principles.body: Where the structure can be the surface, we let it. Fewer layers age more honestly.

principles.title: Draw with light
principles.body: Every plan is also a drawing of the sun's path. Openings are placed for an hour, not an elevation.

principles.title: Build near
principles.body: Materials are sourced as close to site as practical: earth from the excavation, stone from the valley.

projects.title: The Monolithic Void
projects.team: A. Morfis, M. Sørensen, J. Pires
projects.lead: A single mass of board-formed concrete, carved open by one vertical cut of light.
narrative: Set into a granite slope above the Atlantic fog line, the house is conceived as one continuous casting. Its rooms are not built so much as subtracted, a sequence of hollows pressed into the hill.

A single slot, nine metres tall and forty centimetres wide, is the only opening on the entrance façade. Over the course of a day its blade of light travels across the hall, the stair and the dining table, a slow sundial for the household.
Every surface carries the grain of the pine boards it was cast against. Nothing is cladded, nothing is painted; the structure is the finish.

figures.caption: Entrance hall, the nine-metre light slot
The house seen from the lower terrace

projects.title: Timber Pavilion
projects.team: A. Morfis, L. Kragh, T. Ono
projects.lead: Two hundred and forty spruce fins, tuned to the angle of the northern sun.
narrative: The pavilion is a single gallery, sixty metres long, that runs along the fjord's edge. Its walls are a rhythm of vertical fins in cross-laminated spruce, spaced so that walking its length reads like turning the pages of a book.
On the south the fins close into a solid wall; on the north they open toward the water, admitting only reflected light. Exhibitions are lit by the fjord itself.
The building was prefabricated in eleven sections and assembled on site in nine days, sitting lightly on screw piles that leave the shoreline untouched.

projects.title: House of Clay
projects.lead: Walls of rammed earth dug from the site itself, half a metre thick and cool at noon.
narrative: In the Alentejo plain, summer heat is the defining condition. The house answers with mass: rammed-earth walls fifty centimetres thick, compacted in layers from soil excavated for the foundations.
Openings are few and deep. Each frames a single element of the landscape: a cork oak, a well, the horizon line.
Inside, natural clay plaster regulates humidity, and the floors are laid in handmade terracotta fired twenty kilometres away.

figures.caption: Living room, morning light on clay

projects.title: Basalt Archive
projects.team: A. Morfis, M. Sørensen, E. Gunnarsdóttir
projects.lead: A municipal archive wrapped in a deep screen of cast basalt fins.
narrative: The archive holds four centuries of civic records in a climate-stable core, surrounded by a public reading hall that rings the building at street level.

The façade is a screen of cast basalt fins whose depth varies with orientation, deepest to the south and west, so that the reading hall is evenly lit through every season, including the low winter sun.
Construction began in 2025; the building opens in the spring of 2027.

projects.title: Chapel of Still Light
projects.lead: A room for forty people, lit only from above.
narrative: A small chapel on a valley floor, replacing a nineteenth-century oratory lost to a flood. The brief asked only for a room for forty people and a bell.

The walls are local gneiss, laid dry by two masons over one summer. The roof is a single concrete plate held clear of the walls by a band of glass, so that light falls down the stone surfaces rather than into the room.

figures.caption: Light falling along the north wall

projects.title: Courtyard Houses
projects.team: A. Morfis, L. Kragh, C. Ferrer
projects.lead: Eighteen social homes, each organised around its own walled garden.
narrative: Eighteen affordable homes arranged as a low carpet of walled courtyards, a contemporary reading of the Mallorcan patio.
Each house turns inward to a private garden planted with a single tree, and outward to a shared lane shaded by pergolas. Walls are built in marès sandstone quarried on the island.
